From LangChain
to langgraphR

Welcome. Today: what LangChain is, why LangGraph was created, why you can't rebuild it purely in R, and how langgraphR bridges the gap with a hidden Python server.
01
The Foundation
What LangChain is — and what it is not.
We start from the beginning: LangChain, the framework that started it all.

What is LangChain and how it works

What it is

LangChain is a framework that helps you build apps with LLMs. On their own, LLMs just take text in and return text out — LangChain lets you connect them to things like your own documents, databases, memory, and external tools, and chain multiple steps together into a workflow.

At its core, it's just Python code that:

  1. Formats your input into a prompt string the AI can understand
  2. Makes an API call to the AI model (OpenAI, Anthropic, etc.)
  3. Gets the response back and parses it into something usable
  4. Passes it to the next step if there is one
That's genuinely all it's doing under the hood — a wrapper around API calls, with some glue code to connect them together.
1 · Formats your input

Turn user text into a prompt

The user types: "My order hasn't arrived in 2 weeks"

LangChain turns it into: "You are a helpful support agent. A customer said: 'My order hasn't arrived in 2 weeks'. Write a polite reply."

2 · Makes an API call

Send it to the model

LangChain sends that prompt to OpenAI's API behind the scenes.

3 · Gets the response

Read and clean the reply

OpenAI returns: "Hi, we're sorry to hear that. Let us look into your order right away..."

LangChain grabs that text and cleans it up.

4 · Passes it on

Feed the next step

LangChain feeds that reply into the next step — maybe another prompt: "Now translate this reply into French."

LangChain is a thin wrapper: format a prompt, call the model, parse the reply, pass it on. That is the whole trick.

Where chains hit a wall

There was a real problem.

LangChain is built around linear chains — step 1 → step 2 → step 3. That works fine for simple flows. But as people started building more complex AI agents, they hit a wall:

  • What if the AI needs to loop back and retry a step?
  • What if it needs to branch — do this if X, do that if Y?
  • What if you need the AI to pause and wait for a human to approve something before continuing?

LangChain couldn't handle these well because it only moves forward in a straight line.

So they created LangGraph, which models your workflow as a graph — with nodes (steps) and edges (connections) — meaning you can now loop, branch, and build agents that make decisions about what to do next rather than just following a fixed sequence.

In short — LangChain was too rigid for complex agents, and LangGraph was the fix.
LangChain = linear chains. Real agents need loops, branches, and human pauses. LangGraph = graphs that can do all three.
02
LangGraph
Orchestration, done at the right level.
The answer to the chain problem: stop thinking in lines, start thinking in graphs.

LangGraph

LangGraph lets you build AI workflows as a graph — meaning the AI can loop, branch, and make decisions, not just follow a straight line.

How it works:

  • You define nodes — each node is a step (call the AI, check something, run a tool)
  • You define edges — which node to go to next, and under what condition
  • The AI moves through the graph, and based on the result it can go forward, loop back, or take a different path

Real world example — a support ticket bot:

  1. User submits a complaint
  2. AI reads it and decides — is this a billing issue or a technical issue?
  3. If billing → go to the billing node → draft a billing response
  4. If technical → go to the technical node → draft a technical response
  5. If unclear → loop back and ask the user a follow up question
  6. Final response sent to user
In LangChain you couldn't do step 5 — it would just keep moving forward. LangGraph lets it loop back when it's not sure, which makes it much more like how a real agent thinks.
LangGraph = nodes (steps) + edges (transitions). The right-side example shows the loop a chain can't express.

The hard truth

Why you can't build this purely in R

So why not just rewrite LangGraph in R? Because the hard parts of LangGraph are things R was never designed to do.

1

It's built on Python's async engine

The heart of LangGraph is an event loop that juggles many tasks at once. R's standard library has nothing like it. You would have to build that engine yourself before you could build the agent on top.

2

There's no way to stream from a model

A fast agent shows its answer word by word over a streaming connection. Base R has no built-in HTTP client that can read that stream, so the first word can't appear until the whole answer is done.

3

It needs to run 24/7

LangGraph works best as a small server that stays alive and holds many conversations at once. R is designed around short, one-at-a-time sessions — the opposite of what an orchestrator needs.

4

You'd be rewriting a framework, not writing an app

LangGraph is not one function; it's a whole runtime — graph execution, checkpoints, interrupts, streaming. Porting all of that to R is a project by itself, and then you'd have to keep it in sync with the Python version forever.

5

The ecosystem lives in Python

The things you plug in — model APIs, tool-calling, tracing and monitoring — are all Python-first. Even if you got the core running in R, you'd be fighting the ecosystem the whole time.

Bottom line: you wouldn't be writing an R app — you'd be maintaining a port of a Python runtime, forever chasing upstream.

Reaching other languages from R

R doesn't have to stay in R. Through bridges and wrappers, you can write R and reach into other languages — Python, Java, C++ — so you can use their libraries and frameworks (like LangGraph) from inside R.

What is a bridge?

A bridge connects R to another language and translates between them. You write R, it's converted and forwarded to Python (or Java, C++), and the results come back as R objects — so the two languages can talk to each other.

What is a wrapper?

A wrapper is a layer of R functions on top of a foreign library or framework. You call the wrapper's R functions, and it quietly forwards your call to the real library underneath — you never write the other language yourself.

Reticulate

Reticulate is an R package that lets you run Python code inside R. So you write R, but you can call Python libraries like LangGraph directly from within your R script.

Bridges and wrappers let R reach other languages and their frameworks. reticulate is the R package that runs Python from R.

langgraphR: what it is & how it works

langgraphR is an R package that wraps LangGraph. You describe an AI agent as a graph using plain R, and a hidden Python server runs the real LangGraph underneath — so you get loops, memory, and human approval without ever leaving R.

R · your code
Load library(langgraphr), then describe the agent with lg_graph(), lg_add_node(), lg_add_edge() — or chat through LgAgent.
R client
lg_connect() starts a hidden Python server (FastAPI) if it isn't already running.
Python sidecar
It turns your R-described graph into a real LangGraph graph. Nodes, edges, loops and branches. When a node needs R code, it interrupts, R runs the function, and the run resumes.
Model + memory
DeepSeek / OpenAI answer the LLM calls; SQLite checkpoints save state so runs survive a crash.
Architecture: R code → R client (lg_connect boots FastAPI) → Python sidecar (compiles + runs LangGraph, interrupting to run R) → model + SQLite memory.
STEP 1Write your graph in R — each node is an R function
"Writing your graph" is just writing R code. Each step is one of your own R functions — that function is called a node. A graph = your R functions plus the arrows that connect them.
↓
STEP 2lg_compile() sends the blueprint to Python
lg_compile() packages your graph into a description — the blueprint: which nodes exist and how they connect. It sends that to Python so Python can build the same graph.
↓
STEP 3graph$invoke('question') starts the run
graph$invoke() is how you actually run the graph. You pass in the input (a "question"), and it tells the server to start from the first node with that question as the starting state.
↓
STEP 4Python starts, pauses at the first node, sends state to R
Python starts the run, but it can't execute R code. So it pauses at the first node and sends the current state (including your question) back to R, asking R to run that node.
↓
STEP 5R runs YOUR node function — lg_call_model() → LLM
R looks up the node function you wrote and runs it with the state it was given. Inside it you can do anything R can do — including calling the LLM with lg_call_model().
↓
STEP 6R sends the result + next-node choice back
R packages up whatever the function returned (the updated state) plus a hint about which node should run next, and sends it all back to Python.
↓
STEP 7Any more nodes?
Python checks: is there another node to run, or did it say __end__? If another node, the loop continues — Python pauses there and asks R again.
↺ yes → next node pauses → back to STEP 5
↓ no
STEP 8'__end__' → Python sends the final state
When a node returns __end__, Python knows the graph is done. It stops looping and sends the final state back to R.
↓
STEP 9You read res$state$answer
Back in R, the run returns a result object. You read your answer from it — here, res$state$answer.
Each row pairs a flowchart box (left) with its plain-English explanation (right), so every description lines up exactly with its step.
